learning_objective: The learner will critique a described evaluation by judging each of 8 statements about it as a flaw or not a flaw, with at least 7 of 8 correct.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** design-flaw-finder
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/statistics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/experimental-designs-compare
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** critique
**Learning Objective:** The learner will critique a described evaluation by judging each of 8 statements about it as a flaw or not a flaw, with at least 7 of 8 correct. **Prerequisites:** evaluation question, controlled variables, fixed inputs, repeated runs, sample size, fair comparison, bias, limitations statement (all defined in this chapter and in Chapter 20). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner reads the described evaluation, then judges each of 8 statements as "Flaw" or "Not a flaw" before the sim reveals the answer. A judgment is correct when it equals the Correct judgment column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Re-reading the description is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A comparison of two systems needs no controls if one is clearly stronger. (2) A single run is enough to rank. (3) A result scored by the system that produced it is neutral. (4) Having a method is the same as having a fair method. **Instructional Rationale:** Evaluating a design needs criteria applied to a case, so the description contains five real flaws and three sound practices, which prevents answering "flaw" to everything. **Content:** The described evaluation, shown in full to the learner: "A team compares a local model and a cloud model on textbook generation. They run the local model once on Monday on a machine that is also running a database backup, using the Algebra I course description, with the same harness and the same skills as the cloud run. They run the cloud model once on Friday using a rewritten course description that adds a glossary requirement. They score both outputs with the cloud model that wrote the cloud result. The team recorded the model names, versions, and dates of both runs, and stated its evaluation question before running anything. They report that the cloud model is better, without further comment." | # | Statement shown to the learner | Correct judgment | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Each model was run once. | Flaw | One run gives no estimate of run variance, so a difference may be noise. | | 2 | The two runs used different course descriptions. | Flaw | The inputs were not fixed, so a difference could come from the description and not the model. | | 3 | The local model ran while a backup ran on the same machine. | Flaw | Competing load is an uncontrolled variable that can slow or starve the run. | | 4 | Both runs used the same harness and the same skills. | Not a flaw | Holding these fixed is exactly what a fair comparison requires. | | 5 | The cloud model's output was scored by the cloud model that wrote it. | Flaw | A model judging its own work is a source of bias, so the score is not neutral. | | 6 | The team recorded the model names, versions, and dates of both runs. | Not a flaw | A record of the configuration is what makes an experiment reproducible. | | 7 | The team stated its evaluation question before running anything. | Not a flaw | Fixing the question first prevents choosing a measure after seeing the data. | | 8 | The result was reported as "the cloud model is better" with no limitations. | Flaw | A claim from one run per side needs a limitations statement that says so. | **Provenance:** The described evaluation and statements are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The criteria come from the sections of this chapter above. **Rules:** Statements are shown in the fixed order 1 to 8. Each allows one final judgment, and exactly one of "Flaw" or "Not a flaw" is correct for each. The description contains five flaws and three sound practices. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the described evaluation. 2. The learner reads statement 1 and chooses "Flaw" or "Not a flaw", then confirms. 3. The sim shows the correct judgment and the Why text, and marks the statement correct or incorrect. 4. The learner repeats for statements 2 to 8. After statement 8 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss. **Feedback:** Eight statements, fixed order, one confirmed judgment each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct judgment and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 8 correct". **Starting State:** The described evaluation is shown with statement 1 beneath it and no judgment made, and the question on screen is "Is this a flaw in the design?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that one run per side gives no run variance, that inputs must be fixed, that uncontrolled load is a variable, that a model should not score its own output, and that a result needs a limitations statement.
